findings.what: "A simple analogue meter cannot square anything" is absolute and untrue of moving-iron and electrodynamometer meters, whose deflection follows the square so they read rms and which are common on switchboards; say "a common analogue meter (a moving coil with a rectifier)" or "many analogue meters", as Kuphaldt's meter quote supports.

findings.where: Screens 9, 10 and 12, and the explanation's "Textbooks add that a simple analogue meter's needle follows the average"
findings.what: The meter facts (the needle follows the average, and the calibration assumes a sine) carry no citation, and the sources list lacks Kuphaldt's meter quote from research notes 5.1 ("naturally proportional to the average value of the AC ... The accuracy of this calibration depends on an assumed waveshape, usually a sine wave"), so add it as a source and cite it.

findings.where: Practice, first bullet ("Read an AC voltage or current on a label, a nameplate or a meter as rms"), and the explanation's "the usual way the size of an AC voltage or current is given"
findings.what: Both cite [^4], which only defines the DC equivalent and says nothing about labels or nameplates; cite OpenStax's "Appliances and devices are commonly quoted with rms values" (research notes 3.2), the source the brief named for this.

findings.where: Screens 7 and 8 (Mains, The top of the wave)
findings.what: Screen 8 asks how high the mains wave climbs one screen after screen 7 has said "about 325 V", so it tests recall rather than the prediction the brief planned ("a prediction screen asks whether 230 V is the top of the wave"); put the question before the reveal.
Screen 6 asks for the 57.7 V the screen 5 demonstration has just slid to, and screen 12 reuses screen 9's 180 V and 188 V; fresh figures, such as another peak, would test transfer rather than memory.
The task never says the meters are in calibration, yet the Why? opens "Both meters are fine", and a fault-finder could fairly pick "faulty"; add "both meters are in calibration" to the task.
The half-cycle average 0.637 of the peak arrives with no rule; one line (2 ÷ π, a hump's area over its width, from Calculus fundamentals' mid-ordinate work, as the brief planned) closes that step.

findings.where: Screen 3 (Why 70.7 V), text and the work line "square and take the mean: 500 W × 10 Ω = 5000 V²"
findings.what: The mean square is worked back from the heat rather than from the wave, so the recipe never shows squaring the wave; show that the squared wave tops out at 100² = 10 000 V² and averages half, 5000 V², with 500 W × 10 Ω as the check.
The 1.11 mark-up (rms ÷ average) is never named as the form factor, the term BTEC lists (brief, notes 2.1) and his later syllabi will use; name it once.
The brief's sourced sea example, a ship's 440 V peaking at 440 × √2 = 622 V (SECONDARY, notes 6.1), is missing; one line labelled as an example would tie the lesson to his path.

The cable analogy (20 A for a quarter of the time heats like a steady 10 A) and the 358 V peak at the 253 V upper limit are his best trade links but live only in the book's explanation, analogy and practice, never on a screen; a line on screen 3 or 8, or in the finish, would bring them in.

"A steady 100 V gives 1000 W, because the wave touches 100 V only for an instant" gives the wrong cause; say "A steady 100 V gives 1000 W all the time, while the wave touches 100 V only for an instant."

findings.where: Screens 7 and 9, ratio readout ("230 V ÷ 325 V = 0.707", "188 V ÷ 325 V = 0.577")
findings.what: Worked by hand from the numbers shown, these give 0.708 and 0.578, because the quotient comes from the unrounded 325.3 V and 187.6 V; show the peak to one decimal or write ≈.

findings.where: Lead line and caption on screens 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12
findings.what: They still describe 10 Ω heaters and "the 100 V peak" while the picture shows 52.9 Ω heaters on 230 V mains; make them name both cards, or follow the card.

The "?" rings sit on the heater zigzags' right ends with the zigzag tail poking out past them, and the key lists AC, AC average heat and DC though none is drawn.
The empty voltage and power graphs, each with "?", fill most of the picture while the two meters (the subject) sit small at the bottom; shrink or drop the empty graphs on this screen.

findings.what: Mid-motion the readout shows whole volts, so it reads 69, 71 and then 70.7, or 70.7, 71 and then 69 as the triangle begins, and looks like a small overshoot; show one decimal while the level moves.

findings.where: All screens, the DC traces and heat bars
findings.what: The DC level and DC power lines are teal and the heat bars fill amber, while CLAUDE.md keeps teal for small labels and amber for what is due, and the brief makes a second trace ink; check this against the D4 tokens or use ink at a second weight.

Their paragraphs run 75 to 95 words (screen 1 is 14 lines at 360 px) and push the picture below the fold; cut to what the picture does not already show (screen 7, for example, repeats the numbers drawn).
